source.title: The Limit of the Batch Size
source.authors: Yang You; Yu-Hui Wang; Huan Zhang; Zhao Zhang; J. Demmel; Cho-Jui Hsieh

record.file_problem: Full text is present, including the appendix; no obvious truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests large and huge batch training and argues that, beyond a workload-dependent boundary, the generalization gap can persist despite longer training and available optimization techniques. Its own batch-size comparisons and qualifications bear directly on V5.
record.gate_note: The study reports batch-size and optimizer comparisons, accuracy results, and longer-training outcomes. Cited results from prior work and hyperparameter values used only to tune runs are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study directly measures held-out performance as batch size increases and tests whether recipe changes and longer training recover it. Its extreme-batch results qualify the adaptation component of V5; it is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors empirically identify a huge/full-batch regime where tested optimization techniques and very long training fail to reach smaller-batch test accuracy. They claim this contradicts the proposed ultra-slow diffusion account and hypothesize an inherent gap. They also report substantial improvements from LARS and recipe changes. Their experiments do not prove impossibility for all techniques or polynomial training budgets.
record.recipe_differences: Study investigates extreme batch sizes and multiple optimizer/learning-rate recipes, including LARS and LAMB; it is not a reproduction of the original fixed-epoch large-batch comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with batch size, optimizer, learning-rate warmup and schedule, optimizer hyperparameter tuning, label smoothing, training duration, and batch-normalization setup.

fits_no_version.finding: Equal travel distance from initialization can lead to different minima; the authors dispute the ultra-slow diffusion explanation at extreme batch sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight displacement or iteration count alone does not determine generalization across batch sizes.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. Some findings are figure-based, though the paper provides textual summaries for many key comparisons. The authors' claim that the gap cannot be closed by current techniques is an empirical extrapolation from tested recipes and budgets.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports other optimizer comparisons and schedule-tuning results, including MNIST Table 3 variants and CIFAR-10 full-batch plots. They are not separately extracted where the text does not give an individual test-accuracy value or where those results are only figure-based without a reported number. Figure 2, Figures 6–7, and Figures 14–17 show additional tuning-region results but do not provide recoverable separate numeric outcomes in the supplied text.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD generalization under the specified limited or broader tuning protocols. Table 3 compares optimizers for batch scaling but does not establish those tuning conditions.
Language models, workloads beyond the three image-classification tasks, and whether other adaptations or larger budgets can eliminate the remaining penalties.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance and its ranking of generalization gaps against alternative measures.
Removing examples selected by label memorization and comparing with random removal.

missing.what: At matched iteration counts, full-batch ImageNet training attains lower training loss than batch-32K training while still failing to match its test accuracy. This separates the residual generalization deficit from failure to optimize training loss.
Batch-256K ImageNet training with distributed/ghost batch normalization still fails to reach the target after extending training from 90 to 500 epochs; R12 captures only the 90-epoch accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: Only V5 is tested. No challenges verdict is warranted against its qualified wording: extreme-batch failures support its penalty clause and limit where adaptations fully recover accuracy. The paper mixes optimization failure with generalization deficits; Figure 10 supplies the clearest evidence that a deficit persists despite lower training loss. No uncertainty estimates establish whether the tiny residual in R14 is meaningful.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under the version's tuning conditions.
Language models; generality beyond the tested MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet image classifiers; whether all listed adaptations remove or shrink the penalty.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other generalization measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring its effect on test accuracy.

rows.subject: ResNet-50 v1.5
rows.operation_detail: Momentum SGD baseline with batch size 819200 for 141 steps, matching the small-batch baseline epoch count.
rows.note: The baseline run is reported to diverge and attain near-chance accuracy.
rows.check: Near-chance accuracy versus 75.9% supports the fixed-epoch batch penalty, rather than reversing it. The baseline recipe already includes learning-rate scaling, cosine decay, clipping and ghost batch normalization; this run also has optimization failure.

rows.subject: ResNet-50 v1.5
rows.operation_detail: Added learning-rate warmup to huge-batch Momentum SGD.
rows.note: Warmup improves accuracy but remains far below the stated target.
rows.check: Warmup improves the huge-batch run, but 2.712% remains far below the 75.9% small-batch reference. Retain that reference alongside the incremental baseline.

rows.subject: ResNet-50 v1.5
rows.operation_detail: Tuned learning rate and warmup epochs for huge-batch Momentum SGD.
rows.note: Authors say grid search roughly matches auto-tuning; the reported result remains far below target.
rows.check: The fixed-epoch penalty remains pronounced at 4.563%. The preceding recipe's 2.712% measures tuning improvement; the batch comparison requires the 75.9% reference.

rows.subject: ResNet-50 v1.5
rows.operation_detail: Added label smoothing to tuned huge-batch Momentum SGD.
rows.note: Authors state accuracy did not increase and did not significantly decrease.
rows.check: The negligible label-smoothing effect is not absence of the batch penalty. Accuracy remains 4.226% versus the 75.9% small-batch reference.

rows.subject: ResNet-50 v1.5
rows.operation_detail: Switched optimizer from Momentum SGD to LARS.
rows.note: The optimizer change improves accuracy substantially but remains far below the 75.9% target.
rows.check: LARS improves the preceding huge-batch recipe, but 18.95% versus 75.9% still shows the fixed-epoch penalty. Preserve both comparisons.

rows.subject: LeNet
rows.operation_detail: LARS huge-batch training with learning-rate warmup and polynomial decay.
rows.note: The paper reports the test error increase from 0.8% to 4.2%.
rows.check: Higher test error supports V5. The reported error increase is explicitly from batch 8K to 32K; the paper also gives 0.8% error for the batch-256 reference. Record these separately. The standard MNIST budget is 30 epochs. Section 3.1 uses a 55K/5K/10K training/validation/test split.

rows.subject: LeNet
rows.operation_detail: LAMB training with extremely long learning-rate warmup and polynomial decay.
rows.note: The recipe stabilizes training and generalizes better, but does not reach the baseline target.
rows.check: The adapted recipe still falls below the smaller-batch target, showing a residual penalty. Section 3.1 presents this in the standard 30-epoch MNIST experiment; the text does not separately restate the budget for this run.

rows.subject: LeNet
rows.operation_detail: LARS with learning-rate warmup and polynomial decay at batch size 819200.
rows.note: Comparator reflects the reported huge-batch ImageNet outcome with the study's best-performing optimizer at that stage.
rows.check: Subject is ResNet-50 v1.5, not LeNet. The below-20% statement summarizes the same huge-batch ImageNet result as R5; merge or remove this duplicate rather than treating it as independent evidence.

rows.subject: ResNet-50 v1.5
rows.operation_detail: LARS huge-batch training extended to 1200 epochs.
rows.note: Longer training improves the huge-batch result but does not reach the 32K result.
rows.check: Longer training shrinks the deficit substantially, from about 19% to about 70% accuracy, but does not reach 76.7%. This tests adaptation, not a fixed-epoch comparison.

rows.subject: ResNet-50 v1.5
rows.operation_detail: Extended huge-batch training from 3000 to 10000 epochs.
rows.note: Text describes a plateau; best observed accuracy was 71.8%.
rows.check: Record the best huge-batch accuracy, 71.8%, and the 76.7% batch-32K reference alongside the 3000–10000-epoch plateau. A plateau alone does not quantify the remaining batch penalty.

rows.subject: ResNet-50 v1.5
rows.note: Full-batch best reported accuracy remains below the stated 32K reference.
rows.check: The residual deficit after extended training bears on incomplete recovery through adaptation. It is not a fixed-epoch comparison.

rows.subject: ResNet-50 v1.5
rows.operation_detail: ImageNet training with effective batch size 256K and Ghost Batch Normalization.
rows.baseline: target accuracy not numerically restated here
rows.note: Authors say the target was not reached even after increasing training to 500 epochs; this row records the stated 90-epoch result.
rows.check: At 90 epochs, 65% remains below the 76.7% batch-32K reference discussed in Section 4.1 despite distributed/ghost batch normalization. The separate 500-epoch failure should also be recorded.

rows.subject: ResNet-50 v1.5
rows.operation_detail: Huge-batch training with the Kumar et al. recipe and auto-tuned hyperparameters.
rows.note: Table lists eight hyperparameter settings; 73.37% is the highest stated result.
rows.check: The best tuned 128K result remains below the 75.9% target. This is an explicitly reported best achieved outcome, not merely a hyperparameter selection value. The exact epoch count is not restated in Table 4.

rows.subject: LeNet
rows.note: Paper states this does not match the target accuracy.
rows.check: The remaining deficit is only 0.04 percentage points versus 99.2%, with no uncertainty reported. Also record the optimizer-matched LARS reference of 99.3%. This is nearly complete numerical recovery, despite the authors' description of failing to match the target.

source_check.correct: State: observed for V5's longer-training recovery clause. Accuracy reaches 99.16% after 1000 epochs versus 99.2% for batch-256 Momentum SGD and 99.3% for batch-256 LARS after 30 epochs; numerical recovery is nearly complete, without reported uncertainty.
source_check.problem: The partial state understates nearly complete numerical recovery under the state table's full-or-nearly-so rule.

rows.subject: LeNet
rows.note: Text says full-batch accuracy is lower and notes batch size 256 reaches this level in 10 epochs.
rows.check: A residual penalty after longer training is consistent with V5, rather than reversed. Include the LARS small-batch reference of 99.3% as well as the SGD reference of 99.2%.

rows.subject: ResNet-50
rows.note: The paper says full-batch training cannot reach the baseline target even after long training.
rows.check: The extended-training result retains a 1.32-percentage-point deficit. It tests incomplete recovery through longer training rather than the fixed-epoch clause. Specify ResNet-50 v1.
